_metadata.independence: I read only x13-rb-input.json (plus re-reading it in a scratch script solely to verify pair_ids and hint texts match); no other repository file, search, web or paid API was used.

hints.reason: AMERICA via the name Captain America, SHIELD via his iconic round shield; one huge Marvel reference that lands both instantly.

pairs.pair_note: Clean, easy shared reference; fine as is.

hints.reason: BEACH via the Beach Boys, BAND both because the Beach Boys are a band and via the everyday phrase 'boy band', which gives BAND an independent second route the text does not mention.
hints.fix: BAND line: "The Beach Boys are a band, and so is any boy band."

pairs.pair_note: Works better than a plain 'name contains the target' join because 'boy band' independently reaches BAND; worth saying so in the line.

hints.reason: GUITAR via the guitar solo (strong), BAND via solos taken inside a band and the familiar contrast of a singer leaving the band to go solo; the BAND side is softer but honest.

pairs.pair_note: The 'going solo vs. staying in the band' idea is the more satisfying BAND route; the explanation could lean on it, but the current text is accurate.

hints.reason: BAND via Guns N' Roses as a classic rock band, JUNGLE via their signature hit 'Welcome to the Jungle' (a stadium and sports staple); it takes a beat to get from GUNS to the band, but it clicks hard once it does.

pairs.pair_note: Category (BAND) plus a famous song title; the song is widely known even to non-fans. Fair for a general U.S. audience, though the bare word GUNS needs the leap to the band name.

hints.reason: ROCK via 'rock and roll' is instant, but BAND is reached only by tacking 'band' onto the whole phrase (or a stretch to 'drum roll'); ROLL on its own does not call up BAND.

pairs.pair_note: GARAGE (garage band, garage rock) would be a true two-sided phrase join for this pair; ROLL leans almost entirely on ROCK.

hints.reason: BAND via 'rock band' and STAR via 'rock star', both instantly familiar phrases that also belong to one coherent world.

pairs.pair_note: Easy but clean; the two phrases reinforce each other thematically, which lifts it above a bare phrase join.

hints.reason: BASEBALL via sliding into a base, PARK via the playground slide; a clear verb/noun double meaning.

pairs.pair_note: Solid double meaning.

hints.reason: HAND via the palm of the hand, BEACH via palm trees; a classic, clean double meaning.

pairs.pair_note: Classic; nothing to change.

hints.reason: BEE via the queen bee, CHESS via the queen piece (accurately called the strongest); both instant.

pairs.pair_note: Classic and accurate.

hints.reason: BEE via bees buzzing, PHONE via a vibrating phone buzzing; both are the everyday sense of the word.
hints.fix: Bees buzz, and so does a phone on vibrate.

pairs.pair_note: Minor wording: a phone buzzes on vibrate; 'on silent' can mean no vibration at all on some phones.

hints.reason: BIRTHDAY via the cone party hat, MAGIC via the magician's top hat and the rabbit pulled from it; both iconic images.

pairs.pair_note: Easy, pleasant; HAT is broad on a board but both targets are the most iconic hats.

hints.reason: GHOST via Ghostbusters, BLOCK via Blockbuster (the movie term and the video store); two instantly familiar names with a fun nostalgic snap.
hints.fix: Ghostbusters and Blockbuster are both built on the word "buster."

pairs.pair_note: A phrase join that earns its PASS: both compounds are household names. Explanation is slightly off because Ghostbusters ends in 'busters', not 'buster'.

hints.reason: BOX via the jack-in-the-box toy, CAR via the car jack used to change a tire; two distinct, familiar senses.

pairs.pair_note: Good double meaning. Note JACK is also used for CARD + GIANT in this batch; avoid both on one board.

hints.reason: BUBBLE via bubbles popping, MUSIC via pop music; classic double meaning.

pairs.pair_note: Classic.

hints.reason: CAR via its wheels, CHEESE via a wheel of cheese; the cheese side gives a small pleasant surprise.

pairs.pair_note: Good.

hints.reason: CARD via the jack playing card, GIANT via Jack and the Beanstalk; a fairy tale plus a deck of cards is a satisfying aha.

pairs.pair_note: Strong. Shares the hint JACK with BOX + CAR; keep them off the same board.

hints.reason: VIDEO GAME via Mario as gaming's best-known hero, CASTLE via Bowser's castles and the famous 'princess is in another castle' line.
hints.fix: VIDEO GAME line: "Mario is one of the most famous video game heroes."

pairs.pair_note: Strong. 'The most famous' is a defensible but arguable superlative; 'one of the most famous' is safer.

hints.reason: CHESS via the king piece, LION via 'king of the jungle' (and The Lion King); both instant.

pairs.pair_note: 'King of the jungle' is an idiom, not a habitat claim, so the line is fine.

hints.reason: CHOCOLATE via a chocolate bar, GOLD via a gold bar; both are the most common pairing for the word.

pairs.pair_note: BAR is broad on a board, but both targets are its strongest partners. COIN (chocolate coins, gold coins) is an equally good alternative, not clearly better.

hints.reason: DOG via the Dalmatian puppies of 101 Dalmatians, COAT via her scheme to make a fur coat from them; one iconic villain covers both.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent family-film clue; accurate.

hints.reason: DOG via teaching a dog tricks, MAGIC via a magic trick; clean and fair.

pairs.pair_note: Good.

hints.reason: EYE via 'eye patch', PIRATE via the stock image of a pirate wearing one; both arrive together.

pairs.pair_note: Easy, clean.

hints.reason: LION via a pride of lions, FAMILY because a pride is essentially a lion family (plus family pride); a nice indirect aha.

pairs.pair_note: The stronger FAMILY route is 'a pride is a lion family group' rather than 'taking pride in your family'; the current text is accurate, just undersells it.

hints.reason: SUN via sun rays, FISH via rays such as the stingray; clean double meaning.
hints.fix: FISH line: "A ray, like a stingray, is a flat-bodied fish."

pairs.pair_note: 'Flat fish' could be confused with flatfish (flounder, halibut), a different group; 'flat-bodied fish' is precise.

hints.reason: FLOWER via the flower's stem, SCIENCE via STEM education (science, technology, engineering and math); a satisfying click.
hints.fix: A flower has a stem, and STEM stands for science, technology, engineering and math.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; the text should spell out the full acronym rather than 'science and math'.

hints.reason: Both FOOT and RABBIT via the lucky rabbit's foot charm; one familiar superstition holds the pair together.

pairs.pair_note: LUCKY also suggests clovers or horseshoes, but the rabbit's foot is the charm that contains both targets; fair.

hints.reason: Both sides go only through the title Star Fox (FOX by completing the name, VIDEO GAME because it is a game); Star Fox is known to gamers but less so to a general audience, and STAR is such a broad word that it rarely calls up this title first.

pairs.pair_note: Facts are correct (Fox McCloud). The issue is that STAR fans out in every direction on a 28-word board. TAILS (the fox from Sonic, and a fox's tail) is a possible alternative but not clearly better; uncertain how well Star Fox lands with non-gamers.

hints.reason: GHOST via the classic bedsheet ghost costume, PAPER via a sheet of paper; two clear senses.
hints.fix: A bedsheet makes a classic ghost costume, and paper comes in sheets.

pairs.pair_note: Good idea; explanation wording 'and so is paper' is awkward.

hints.reason: GUM via bubble gum, SOAP via soap bubbles; both everyday.

pairs.pair_note: Easy, fine.

hints.reason: VIDEO GAME only via recalling the title Animal Crossing from its second word, ISLAND via the island setting of New Horizons specifically; CROSSING alone suggests crosswalks or railroads first, so the player must do real work.
hints.fix: In Animal Crossing: New Horizons, you build a life on a deserted island.

pairs.pair_note: New Horizons was a mainstream hit, so the reference is fair once explained, but a title fragment as hint is a weak phrase join; earlier Animal Crossing games were set in villages, so the text should name New Horizons.

hints.reason: KING via the royal crown, TOOTH via a dental crown; the dental sense gives a real 'oh, nice'.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent.

hints.reason: KNIGHT via a knight's shield, POLICE via riot shields and the badge-as-'shield' usage from cop shows; the badge sense is mostly NYPD/TV slang, but riot shields make the POLICE side broadly reachable.
hints.fix: A knight carries a shield, and police carry riot shields and often call their badges shields.

pairs.pair_note: Accurate as written (NYPD badges are called shields), but adding riot shields gives most players the easier route.

hints.reason: PUMPKIN via the jack-o'-lantern, LIGHT because a lantern is a light (and the jack-o'-lantern is lit inside); clean.

pairs.pair_note: Good; the jack-o'-lantern ties both sides together.

hints.reason: OWL via Hedwig being Harry's snowy owl, MAIL via her delivering his letters; Harry Potter is mainstream and Hedwig is one of its best-known characters.

pairs.pair_note: Not niche fandom: Hedwig and owl post are among the most widely known Harry Potter details.

hints.reason: MOVIE via the movie screen, WINDOW via the window screen that keeps bugs out; two distinct senses.

pairs.pair_note: Good.

hints.reason: RAT via Splinter being a rat, NINJA via his role as the Ninja Turtles' sensei; TMNT is broadly known in the U.S.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; the everyday meaning of 'splinter' makes the TMNT click satisfying.

hints.reason: OCEAN via the ocean choosing Moana, PRINCESS via her place in the official Disney Princess lineup; both accurate.

pairs.pair_note: Accurate and broad.

hints.reason: PIRATE via the pirate flag (Jolly Roger), SKULL via the skull and crossbones on it; FLAG is broad, but the pirate flag is an iconic image.

pairs.pair_note: CROSSBONES would be more pointed but also more obvious; FLAG is fine.

hints.reason: SOLDIER via Mulan disguising herself to serve in the army, PRINCESS via her official Disney Princess status; the text carefully says 'counted among', which is accurate since she is not royalty.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; the soldier/princess contrast is part of the fun.

hints.reason: ROPE via knots tied in rope, TIE both via tying a knot and via the necktie knot (Windsor etc.); close to one sense of TIE but honestly connects both.

pairs.pair_note: KNOT is near a synonym of the verb 'tie', but the necktie route keeps it a real two-sided clue.

hints.reason: SNAKE via the game Snake preloaded on Nokia phones, VIDEO GAME because Snake is the famous phone game; a nostalgic aha that most adults recognise.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent indirect clue; younger players may know it as a meme, which still works.

hints.reason: SUN via a sunbeam, WOOD via a wooden beam; two distinct senses of the word.

pairs.pair_note: Good.
